hook.line: Nobody at the café knows what Altamira will do next, so half of every conversation is *maybe*. Spanish has three ways to say it, and one of them is a trap: two take the wish form, one never does.
hook.es: A lo mejor Vale viene mañana.

examples.es: A lo mejor Vale viene mañana.

examples.en: Maybe you're right, I think you are. (to a friend)
Maybe you're right, who knows. (to a friend)

examples.es: A lo mejor Hernando tiene hambre.

rule:
Three ways to say *maybe*:
*A lo mejor* + plain verb, always: *A lo mejor viene*.
*Quizás* + either verb.
*Tal vez* + either verb.

With *quizás* and *tal vez* you choose. The plain verb (*tienes razón*) says you think it is fairly likely. The wish form (*tengas razón*) says you are less sure, more "who knows".

*A lo mejor* has no choice: plain verb, every time. *A lo mejor tengas razón* is a classic mistake.

Safe habit: if you are not sure which to use, say *a lo mejor* and the plain verb. It is the easiest one.

English just says "maybe" and keeps the verb. Spanish lets the verb carry how sure you are.
smallPrint: Teachers call this the mood choice after adverbs of possibility: *quizás* and *tal vez* take the indicative or the subjunctive, while *a lo mejor* takes only the indicative.

readAndPick.es: A lo mejor Vale viene mañana.

options: I doubt you're right. (to a friend)
Maybe you're right, and I think it's fairly likely. (to a friend)

readAndPick.es: A lo mejor llueve más tarde.

yourTurn.prompt: Pick *viene* or *venga* and type the whole sentence: *A lo mejor Vale ___ mañana.*
yourTurn.answer: A lo mejor Vale viene mañana.
yourTurn.why: *A lo mejor* never takes the wish form, so the plain verb: *viene*.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: Maybe Hernando is hungry. Use *a lo mejor*.
yourTurn.answer: A lo mejor Hernando tiene hambre.
yourTurn.why: *A lo mejor* plus the plain verb: *tiene*.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish, to a friend: Maybe you're right (fairly likely). Use *tal vez* and the plain verb.
yourTurn.why: The plain verb after *tal vez* says you think it is likely.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish, to a friend: Maybe you're right (not sure). Use *tal vez* and the wish form.
yourTurn.why: The wish form after *tal vez* says you are less sure.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: Maybe it'll rain later. Use *a lo mejor*.
yourTurn.answer: A lo mejor llueve más tarde.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: Maybe Vale will come tomorrow. Use *quizás* and the wish form.
yourTurn.why: *Quizás* lets you choose, and the wish form of *venir* is *venga*.

yourTurn.prompt: Change *Quizás Hernando tenga hambre* so it starts with *A lo mejor*.
yourTurn.answer: A lo mejor Hernando tiene hambre.
yourTurn.why: *A lo mejor* has no choice, so *tenga* goes back to *tiene*.

pitfalls.wrong: A lo mejor Vale venga mañana.
pitfalls.right: A lo mejor Vale viene mañana.
pitfalls.why: Almost. *A lo mejor* never takes the wish form: always the plain verb.
Almost. Same rule: with *a lo mejor* the plain verb is the only choice.

pitfalls.wrong: A lo mejor que Vale viene mañana.
pitfalls.right: A lo mejor Vale viene mañana.
pitfalls.why: Almost. English can say "maybe that", but *a lo mejor* is complete on its own: no *que* after it.

personal: Think of one plan you might have this weekend but are not sure about. Say it with *A lo mejor*, then again with *quizás* and the wish form.
